beats.script_body: This walk begins at what was the city hall of the City of Brooklyn until 1898, and ends at what has been the City Hall of New York City since 1812. Confused? Brooklyn and New York were separate cities until 1898, when they were consolidated into Greater New York, the current five boroughs. In that year, Brooklyn's 1849 City Hall was renamed Borough Hall, and a cupola was added to make it appear more like New York's City Hall. The building was originally designed in the spirit of common-man Jeffersonian democracy by Brooklyn carpenter and grocer Gamaliel King.

beats.script_body: The idea of Brooklyn joining New York was contentious, much as Staten Island's threat to secede was in the mid-1990s. The consolidation referendum passed by only a few hundred votes in 1894. Many prominent Brooklyn citizens didn't want to merge what they saw as corrupt New York with pristine Brooklyn. After the referendum passed, a group of businessmen, including A. A. Low and Henry Pierrepont, two of the city's wealthiest landowners, along with cultural and religious leaders, formed the League of Loyal Citizens to oppose consolidation. Their vision of Brooklyn was of a white, prosperous, Protestant borough that wasn't teeming with Manhattan's immigrants. The League's spokesperson was St. Clair McKelway, editor of the Brooklyn Eagle, which sponsored an anticonsolidation song contest. "Up with the Flag of Brooklyn" won the three-hundred-dollar prize. McKelway wrote an editorial against consolidation in 1894, warning that "Brooklyn is a city of homes and churches. New York is a city of Tammany Hall and crime government," and that if tied to New York, Brooklyn would become "a Tammany suburb, to be kicked, looted and bossed as such." In spite of the League's opposition, Brooklyn and New York were joined.

beats.script_body: The "park" stretching into the distance is Cadman Plaza, the eastern border of Brooklyn Heights. The Heights was the city's first historic district, though you wouldn't know it from the unattractive high-rises that surround Cadman Plaza; if not for historic preservation, all of Brooklyn Heights might look like them. Before the 1965 historic district law, property owners and the city could and did destroy homes at will. In 1953, construction for Robert Moses's Brooklyn-Queens Expressway razed parts of Columbia Heights, Middagh Street, and Poplar Street. Cadman Plaza itself destroyed much of the eastern Heights, including the building in which Walt Whitman set the type for the first edition of Leaves of Grass. In the face of all this destruction, a group of neighborhood residents formed the Community Conservation and Improvement Council, pronounced "kick," in 1958. CCIC joined with the Brooklyn Heights Association in 1959 and proposed a historic zoning designation modeled on Boston's Beacon Hill. In January 1965 the U.S. Department of the Interior declared the Heights a historic district, and in April the New York City Landmarks Preservation Law passed. Brooklyn Heights was the first such neighborhood in New York, predating Greenwich Village. The reason the Heights still looks as it does is that a band of citizens fought to make it so.

beats.script_body: Spencer Memorial Church, from 1853, stands on the southeast corner of Remsen and Clinton. Built as the First Presbyterian Church of Brooklyn, its first minister was Ichabod Spencer, hence the name. Because the Heights was developed as an idyllic suburban enclave whose promoters emphasized its respectable character, they saw to it that churches were erected wherever possible. Brooklyn was sometimes called the "borough of churches." The church is now a group of co-op apartments.

beats.script_body: In addition to banks, Montague was the original site of three of Brooklyn's greatest cultural institutions, all now demolished but rebuilt elsewhere in the borough. The 1864 Mercantile Library sat on the north side of the block; it eventually merged with the Brooklyn Public Library, which moved to Grand Army Plaza in 1941. To the south was the 1872 Brooklyn Art Association, a forerunner to the Brooklyn Museum now on Eastern Parkway. And the Brooklyn Academy of Music had its opening night here in 1861, before relocating east to the neighborhood of Fort Greene.

beats.script_body: On the northwest corner of Montague and Clinton stands the 1847 Church of St. Ann and the Holy Trinity, whose stained-glass windows were made by William Jay Bolton. Supposedly Bolton left America for England after finishing these windows, never to work in stained glass again. Many years later one of his elderly surviving daughters, nearing the end of her life, discovered her father's past and journeyed to Brooklyn Heights to see the work. Seeing the windows inspired her to live another ten years.

beats.script_body: The 1880 Brooklyn Historical Society stands on the southwest corner of Pierrepont and Clinton. Its architect was George Post, who also designed the New York Stock Exchange Building. The society began in 1863 as the Long Island Historical Society and today houses one of the most extensive regional collections in the country. On the building's facade are busts of Christopher Columbus and Benjamin Franklin, and flanking the entranceway are the heads of an Indian and a Viking. On the east side are numerous other heads and an inscription from Cicero translated as "History, the Witness of Time."

beats.script_body: 5 Montague Terrace is where Thomas Wolfe lived from 1933 to 1934 and finished Of Time and the River. A friend described his rooms: the chief piece of furniture was an old table, work-worn and ancient, marked by cigarette burns, its surface dented like a shield after a hard battle. Opposite the windows stood a gas range and an electric refrigerator that bumped and hummed; Wolfe claimed the rhythm of that sound stimulated him, and on the old table and on the refrigerator he did most of his writing.

beats.script_body: Two of three original mansions designed by Richard Upjohn in 1857 still stand near the playground. Farthest south, at 3 Pierrepont Place, was the former home of Abiel Abbott Low, a merchant who got rich trading with China and moved to the Heights in the mid-nineteenth century. His son Seth Low was the only person to be mayor of both Brooklyn, in 1884, and New York City, in 1901, and later became president of Columbia University. The next mansion, at No. 2, was the home of Alfred Tredway White, a wealthy merchant and philanthropist whose charitable motto was "Philanthropy plus 5 percent"; White funded model tenements for the poor in Brooklyn. The playground next door is all that remains of the third Upjohn mansion, demolished in 1946, which had been the home of Henry Pierrepont, whose family owned much of the surrounding land early in the nineteenth century.

beats.script_body: Standing on the Promenade looking out over the harbor to downtown Manhattan, you have a modern version of the view that merchants like A. A. Low had 150 years ago, when they wanted to look upon their business on South Street in New York. From here you can also see why the neighborhood is called the Heights; many streets that end at the Promenade once sloped down to the shoreline. And from here, in 1776, George Washington evacuated Long Island, fleeing with his troops across to Manhattan under cover of fog and then northward to Harlem and out of New York, which was occupied by the British for the entire course of the Revolutionary War.

beats.script_body: Willow Street shows off most of the architectural styles in the Heights. On your left are Gothic revival townhouses of the 1830s and 1840s, given away by the large blocks of their outer walls and Tudor arched windows. Further along on the right, 109 Willow is a Colonial revival building with exposed outside shutters, while across the street 108-112 Willow is a Queen Anne building from the 1880s, mixing terra-cotta, shingles, bay windows, gables, and a small tower into a bizarre style that somehow works. At the southeast corner of Clark stands 101 Willow, an excellent 1838 Greek revival home with a Greek Ionic portico over the front door and a high basement; its current owner had bricks from the back of the house moved to the front, where they would make it look appropriately aged.

beats.script_body: Look east down Clark to the St. George Hotel, which takes up most of the block between Hicks and Henry. The St. George defined residence-hotel elegance in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Built in stages from 1885 to 1929, it had between twenty-six hundred and twenty-eight hundred rooms, making it the largest hotel in the United States for many years. Many New Yorkers held coming-out parties, weddings, and anniversaries in its giant ballroom, and it was a favored hangout of the Brooklyn Dodgers. Today the St. George has been divided into apartments; its saltwater swimming pool with the mirrored ceiling is gone, replaced by racquetball courts.

beats.script_body: Why is there a Cranberry, an Orange, and a Pineapple Street in Brooklyn Heights? The myth is that Mabel Middagh Hicks, a descendant of two wealthy Brooklyn families, was upset at all the family names on the streets, so she put up her own, more colorful ones, and the Board of Aldermen eventually let them remain. Is it true? We don't know. Another great Heights story, this one not true, concerns Mabel's relatives, the Hicks brothers, "Milk" and "Spitter" Hicks. The family did have a farm here and likely sold produce in Manhattan; supposedly the word hick for a country bumpkin comes from the cry "Here come the Hicks" when the family came to sell vegetables. It's a great story, but "Hick" is actually a seventeenth-century British abbreviation for "Richard."

beats.script_body: The building at 124 Columbia Heights, on the river side of the street, sits atop what was 110 Columbia Heights. Washington Roebling, the chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge, lived in this house for a few years after suffering a nervous breakdown, or a severe case of the bends depending on whom you ask, and watched his bridge go up through a telescope for months at a time. The writer Hart Crane later rented what he was convinced was Roebling's room, from 1924 to 1929. He wrote of the bridge: "And up at the right the Brooklyn Bridge, the most superb piece of construction in the modern world, I'm sure, with strings of light crossing it like glowing worms as the Ls and surface cars pass each other coming and going."

beats.script_body: Across the grass courtyard from the 1849 Italianate Plymouth Church of the Pilgrims, designed by Joseph Wells, stands a statue of the Reverend Henry Ward Beecher. Beecher was America's leading abolitionist, using Christianity to condemn slavery and speaking so widely that extra ferries, called "Beecher's Boats," ran on Sundays to bring listeners from Manhattan to hear him preach. By 1859 he was making thousands yearly as a minister, and both Abraham Lincoln and Mark Twain came to hear him speak. His fame at the time was exceeded only by that of his sister Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, which outsold all books except the Bible in the 1850s. It is hard to impress on the modern reader the national stature of a preacher like Beecher, the authors note: think Billy Graham, Jesse Jackson, and Norman Vincent Peale all rolled into one.

beats.script_body: Henry Ward Beecher was the subject of the "trial of the century" of the 1800s. In 1874 the preacher who advocated high moral standards in others was accused of "alienation of affection": he had had an affair with a married parishioner, Elizabeth Tilton. Beecher hushed the affair up until it was brought into the open by Victoria Woodhull and her sister Tennessee Claflin, both noted equal-rights advocates, spiritualists, investors, and feminists. Woodhull held the radical idea that a woman's sexual needs were equal to a man's and that love should not be controlled by anyone but the parties involved; she called it "free love." Her newspaper, Woodhull and Claflin's Weekly, declared Beecher a closet "free lover" and cleverly linked her struggle for "social freedom" to Beecher's fight against slavery, vowing the article would "burst like a bombshell into the ranks of this moralistic social camp." Woodhull, Claflin, and their publisher were almost immediately jailed for obscenity, though other papers reprinted the charges and no one else was arrested. Beecher's six-month civil trial, brought by Elizabeth's husband Theodore Tilton, became a fascinating entrée into sex, infidelity, and free love in Victorian America. It ended with a hung jury, and two church inquiries exonerated Beecher, though historical evidence has long since shown that he was clearly guilty. A contemporary paper had the last word: "The trial was a fine illustration of the power of money and the tricks that can be played with the law."

beats.trigger_address: Cranberry Street and Cadman Plaza West, Brooklyn Heights
beats.script_body: About where Cranberry used to meet Fulton Street, now Cadman Plaza West, stood the greatest landmark of all in Brooklyn Heights, now gone: here Walt Whitman set the first edition of Leaves of Grass. On Cranberry behind Plymouth Church is the site of one of Whitman's many Brooklyn homes. As he remembered it: "From 1824 to 1828 our family lived in Brooklyn in Front, Cranberry, and Johnson Streets. In the latter my father built a nice house for a home, and afterwards another in Tillary St. We occupied them one after the other, but they were mortgaged, and we lost them." And we have lost them all too, the authors add, including Whitman's printer's and the building where he edited the Brooklyn Daily Eagle.

beats.script_body: The bridge is pregnant with aesthetic symbolism. You're looking at the most ancient material, stone, girded with what was in its time the most modern, steel. A suspension bridge brings together the two great forces in engineering, tension and compression. The steel cables are under nothing but tension as they strain to hold up the bridge; the granite towers are under nothing but compression as they strain to support the massive cables. In a suspension bridge the roadway is hung from cables, which take the load and transmit it to the towers and then to the ground. Anchorages underground on the Brooklyn and Manhattan shorelines hold down the ends of the four cables, each composed of thousands of strands. The deck is hung by yet more steel cables called "suspenders," and diagonal cables called "stays" hold the bridge rigid.

beats.script_body: Suspension bridges of rope, vine, leather, and wood have existed for thousands of years. But it wasn't until the early 1800s that wrought iron could be produced cheaply enough to replace wood, stone, and cast iron, making the modern suspension bridge possible. Even then the iron was first made into a chain and lifted all at once, a feat limited by the chain's weight. It was the idea of "spinning" a cable one strand at a time, making the cables in place, that made possible the suspension bridges we have today.

beats.script_body: Stop when the walkway turns from cement to wood and consider the men who designed the bridge. John Augustus Roebling, born in 1806, grew up in Germany and finished his engineering degree at the Royal Polytechnic Institute in Berlin in 1826; his senior thesis was on suspension bridges, and he also studied with the philosopher Hegel. Like many young men of his generation he left Germany for the United States, where, as he later said, the "hindrances, restrictions, and obstacles" of timid governments "are not to be found." He settled in the Pennsylvania community of Saxonburg and started farming, but soon tired of the fields. Roebling got the idea for wire rope while on an engineering job, noting that the thick hemp ropes used to tow canal boats up inclined railways were expensive and dangerous; metal rope, he believed, would be stronger and cheaper. He was right, and soon had most of the townsfolk making wire rope. In 1848 he moved his family to Trenton and founded a wire-rope company that ran as John A. Roebling's Sons until it was sold in 1953. He went on to build aqueducts, suspension-bridge canals, and a railroad bridge across Niagara Falls, becoming the most famous bridge builder in the United States when the New York Bridge Company chose him as chief engineer in 1867. Roebling, unfortunately, believed in the curative powers of water. While surveying for the anchorages on a Brooklyn dock on June 28, 1869, his foot was crushed against a piling by a docking ferry. He treated the wound by pouring cold water over it and died a month later of tetanus, leaving his thirty-two-year-old son Washington to take over.

beats.script_body: At the Brooklyn tower, look at the plaques illustrating the bridge-building process. From August 1876 to October 1878, after the towers were finished, Roebling's workers spun the cables back and forth across the river. The first strand crossed on August 11, 1876. Two weeks later Master Mechanic E. F. Farrington made the first crossing of the East River by the great bridge, sitting in a boatswain's chair, nothing more than a flat board with a rope loop holding it to a pulley wheel; it took him twenty-two minutes to go from the Brooklyn to the New York side. The Brooklyn Bridge was the first bridge to use steel cables rather than iron. Emily Roebling, born in 1843, was Washington's tireless go-between for communicating instructions to E. F. Farrington and the other engineers on the bridge. He dictated specifications to her, and she carried the information to the assistant engineers. By 1879 she had spent seven years absorbed with the bridge.

beats.script_body: You're now near the midpoint, 135 feet above the high-water mark by order of the War Department, which had to ensure ships built at the Brooklyn Navy Yard upriver could pass beneath. A bridge is a constant invitation to the reckless. The first person to jump from the bridge was Robert Odlum, a Washington, D.C., swimming instructor, who leaped on May 19, 1885, hoping to survive; unfortunately he didn't. The most famous jumper was Steve Brodie, who at age twenty-seven took bets that he could jump and live. He did, or at least said he did. Witnesses claimed he succeeded, and Brodie took his two-hundred-dollar winnings and opened a saloon on the Bowery, where he hung an oil painting of himself jumping and sat beneath it for years telling his story to all comers.

beats.script_body: Remember that the bridge was built before automobiles clogged the streets. It was used by horse carts, pedestrians, and a cable railway running on the two inside lanes. A steam engine on the Brooklyn side powered the cable car on its five-minute, five-cent trip; from one to five in the morning the steam was shut off and locomotives did the work. The cable car was gradually electrified but didn't stop running until 1944, when an electric trolley took over the middle lanes, leaving only the outside lane to horses.

beats.script_body: The Manhattan tower is not standing on bedrock, and how it got here is another story. Excavating the foundations was the most innovative, difficult, and uncertain part of building the bridge. The problem was how to get a foundation onto an area 100 by 170 feet, 44.5 feet beneath the water on the Brooklyn side and 75 feet on the Manhattan side. The solution was caissons, huge bottomless wooden boxes, fifteen feet thick at the top and tapering at the sides. The Brooklyn caisson was 168 by 102 feet, the Manhattan one 172 by 102 feet. They were built in shipyards north of the site, launched like giant barges, floated into place, and anchored with pilings. Compressed air was pumped in to keep the water out except for a foot or so at the bottom. Shafts driven through the roof allowed things in and out: dirt and rocks went out through a water shaft fitted with a giant clamshell-shaped dredging claw, and men entered and left through an airshaft. As the men dug and dynamited downward, masonry was laid on top, sinking the caisson further into the earth. The caissons were lit by sperm-whale-oil candles, the temperature inside eighty degrees and humid. Master mechanic E. F. Farrington said the scene gave one, if of a poetic temperament, "a realizing sense of Dante's inferno." When the workers reached bedrock on the Brooklyn side and hardpan on the Manhattan side, they were pulled out and the caissons filled with concrete.

beats.script_body: Inside the caisson, workers labored in conditions that broke their bodies. Frank Harris, author of My Life and Loves, claimed that as a sixteen-year-old boy he worked there: in a bare shed the men warned him no one could do the work for long without getting the "bends." In the air-lock, as compressed air was turned on, the pain in their ears was so acute the men clapped their hands over them. Below, six of them worked naked to the waist in a small iron chamber at about eighty degrees, sweat pouring within five minutes while they stood in icy water held down only by the terrific pressure; the headaches were blinding, and most men didn't work more than ten minutes at a stretch. Harris said he plugged on, resolved to prove himself, though some historians believe he never actually worked in the caissons at all.

beats.script_body: Take one final look at the bridge. When it opened on May 24, 1883, it was the biggest celebration since the opening of the Erie Canal at the beginning of the century. Tickets for seven thousand guests were issued; fifty thousand more attended; and the celebration began with an hour of fireworks and bands on steamers beneath the bridge. President Chester Arthur and the mayors of both Brooklyn and New York attended, and Emily Roebling led them across. It was a glorious day for New York. One week later, on Memorial Day, twelve pedestrians were trampled to death on a narrow stairway like the one you climbed at the Brooklyn end; the crowd thought the bridge was falling and panicked trying to get off. They were wrong, but it was a tragic end to a masterful building process.

beats.script_body: If you can get close to City Hall when you read this, it means New York City has relaxed restrictions on people getting near the government. Finished in 1811, the building is only the third city hall New York has ever had, and its construction costs came in under the $250,000 budgeted. Originally most of the building was marble, with the north face and basement covered in less-expensive brownstone, because the planners assumed few would view it from the north. But between 1954 and 1956 the top four inches of the entire facade were stripped off and replaced with Alabama veined limestone, the basement redone with red granite, and all the columns, capitals, balustrades, and trim recut in new limestone. The entire facade you see is thus a replica of the original.
